content: Breast self-examination (BSE) is a simple method that can help in the early detection of some types of breast cancer, but it is not a reliable substitute for proven screening methods like mammography. When performed correctly and consistently, BSE may assist in identifying abnormalities, but it should always be complemented by professional medical evaluations. To perform a breast self-examination, follow these steps: 1. Stand in front of a mirror with your upper body exposed. Place your hands on your hips and visually inspect your breasts for any signs of dimpling, swelling, redness, or soreness. 2. Raise your arms above your head and repeat the visual inspection, looking for the same abnormalities. 3. While standing, use your fingers to palpate your breasts. Use the pads of your fingers rather than poking with the tips, and feel both the superficial tissue just beneath the skin and the deeper tissue. Cover the entire breast systematically. One approach is to divide the breast into quadrants and examine each quadrant thoroughly. Don’t forget to check the axillary tail, which is the part of the breast tissue that extends toward the armpit. 4. Repeat the palpation process while lying down, as this position can make it easier to feel certain areas of the breast. 5. Examine the nipples and the area beneath them. Gently squeeze each nipple to check for any discharge. An alternative method for performing BSE is the Seven P's approach, which includes the following steps: 1. Position: Begin by visually inspecting your breasts in front of a mirror with your arms in different positions (at your sides, on your hips, and raised above your head). Then, perform the palpation while lying down, first with a pillow under one shoulder, then under the other, and finally lying flat. 2. Perimeter: 3. Palpation: Use the pads of your fingers to palpate the breast without lifting your fingers as you move across the tissue. 4. 5. Pattern: Choose a systematic pattern for palpation that works best for you. Options include the vertical strip pattern (moving fingers up and down), the pie-wedge pattern (starting at the nipple and moving outward), or the circular pattern (moving in concentric circles from the nipple outward). 6. Practice: Regularly practice BSE to become familiar with the normal feel of your breast tissue. A healthcare provider can offer guidance and feedback on your technique. 7. Plan: Have a clear plan for what to do if you notice any changes in your breast tissue. Be aware of your family history of breast cancer and follow your healthcare provider’s recommendations for mammography. For premenopausal women, it is best to perform BSE at the same point in your menstrual cycle each month, ideally just after your period ends when the breasts are least swollen or tender. Postmenopausal women should perform BSE once a month, such as on the first or last day of the month. It is important to note that approximately 80% of lumps detected through BSE are benign. However, any abnormality should be promptly reported to a healthcare provider for further evaluation. While many breast cancers are first identified by women themselves, BSE should not replace annual clinical breast exams performed by a medical professional. Experts are more likely to detect abnormalities that may be missed during self-examination. Additionally, BSE is not a substitute for more reliable diagnostic tools like mammography or MRI. For more comprehensive and up-to-date information, consult reputable sources such as the Johns Hopkins Breast Cancer Center.
